meta.title: Who really said "It Is the Best Play I Ever Slept Through"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Oscar Wilde probably said it, but not in print: the earliest record is a friend's 1910 memoir, page 132 — not found in Wilde's own writings.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It Is the Best Play I Ever Slept Through'?
meta.ogDescription: The earliest record of Wilde's theatre quip is page 132 of Seymour Hicks's 1910 memoir. Credibly attributed — but found in none of Wilde's own works.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credibly credited to Wilde, and by someone who knew him: the actor-manager Seymour Hicks reports the reply on page 132 of his memoir, first published in London on 26 October 1910. But Quote Investigator ↗ has not located the line anywhere in Wilde’s own writings, so the attribution rests on a single second-hand account published after his death.

source.heading: The earliest record: a friend’s memoir, 1910

docMeta.dd: Seymour Hicks: Twenty-Four Years of an Actor’s Life
London: Alston Rivers, 26 October 1910 · New York: John Lane, 1911
Second-hand anecdote, printed after Wilde’s death

source.excerpt: Innumerable are the witticisms laid at his door. What could be more delightful than his remark to the gushing female admirer who, shaking him warmly by the hand, said: “Oh, but Mr. Wilde, you don’t remember me. My name is Smith.” “Oh yes,” said Wilde, “I remember your name perfectly—but I can’t think of your face.” It was Wilde who, on being asked on returning from a fashionable premiere how he liked the piece, replied: “My dear friend, it is the best play I ever slept through.”
trail: Before 1895 — the window. If Wilde used the quip at all, Quote Investigator ↗ reasons he probably said it before 1895: he was in jail from 1895 to 1897, and his social circumstances changed dramatically afterward.

1898 — the joke in print, but not about a play. The earliest printed instance of the gag that Quote Investigator located is a Denver newspaper report of a sermon by Rev. Myron W. Reed: “It was the most exhaustive lecture I ever slept through.” See the chronology ↗

1910 — the earliest ascription to Wilde. Seymour Hicks prints the remark on page 132 of his memoir, first published in London on 26 October 1910; Quote Investigator cites the John Lane New York printing of 1911 at the same page. Internet Archive scan ↗

1946 — a target is supplied. Hesketh Pearson’s Oscar Wilde: His Life and Wit (page 196) reports the line as Wilde’s verdict on a piece by Arthur Pinero — the first time any play is attached to it. Documented by QI ↗
source.excerptNote: Hicks is recalling, not transcribing. Wilde died in 1900; the memoir’s title page records first publication on 26 October 1910. No play and no playwright is named in this passage.

source.rightsNote: Wilde died in 1900 and his own work is long out of copyright. The book that actually carries this line — Seymour Hicks’s memoir — states first publication on 26 October 1910, comfortably before the 1931 US threshold, and the Internet Archive’s record for the scan lists it as not in copyright.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: Oscar Wilde
author.bio: Oscar Fingal O’Fflahertie Wills Wilde was an Irish author, poet and playwright who became one of London’s most popular dramatists in the early 1890s, with Lady Windermere’s Fan and The Importance of Being Earnest. His public life collapsed with his imprisonment from 1895 to 1897, and he died in 1900. Much of what we quote as “Wilde” is not from his books at all but from his talk — remembered, and written down afterwards, by the people who were in the room.

The line has not been found in Wilde’s own writings.

copyAttribution: "It is the best play I ever slept through." — attributed to Oscar Wilde (1854–1900). Earliest documented in Seymour Hicks, Seymour Hicks: Twenty-Four Years of an Actor's Life (London: Alston Rivers, 1910), p. 132, where Hicks reports it as Wilde's spoken reply on returning from a fashionable premiere. Quote Investigator has not found the line in Wilde's own writings. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What’s true, and what got added later
misattribution.intro: Wilde attracts invented epigrams the way a magnet attracts filings, so it is worth being exact. This one is not a fabrication — but three things routinely said about it go well past the evidence.

items.why: The line is constantly reproduced as Wilde’s devastating one-sentence theatre notice. The only near-contemporary source presents it as speech: Hicks reports Wilde saying it to a friend who asked how he liked the piece on returning from a fashionable premiere. Read page 132 ↗

Hicks names no play and no playwright. The Pinero detail first appears in Hesketh Pearson’s biography Oscar Wilde: His Life and Wit (Harper & Brothers, 1946), page 196, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

“… I ever slept through” was fitted to a lecture in an 1898 Denver sermon report, a picture in 1922, a Presidential message in a Will Rogers column in 1923, an opera in 1929 and a baccalaureate service in 1937 — a chronology assembled by Quote Investigator ↗. The gag travels; the “play” version is the one tied to Wilde.

No letter, essay, review or play of Wilde’s carries this sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ states plainly that it has not located the jape in his writings, while still concluding there is evidence he used it.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: one good witness, no document. Seymour Hicks — who knew Wilde and socialised with him — printed the reply on page 132 of his 1910 memoir, and Quote Investigator ↗ found no earlier ascription to Wilde and no instance in Wilde’s own writing. Credibly attributed; not verified.

context.heading: Why so much “Wilde” comes to us second-hand
lead: Almost everything we have of Wilde the talker arrives the same way: someone who was in the room wrote it down later. He published plays, essays, criticism and one novel, but his conversation — by every contemporary account the better performance — survives mainly in other people’s books.

This line is a clean example of the type. Seymour Hicks was an actor-manager who moved in Wilde’s circle, and in 1910 he set down a handful of Wilde’s remarks from memory, this one among them. As second-hand evidence goes it is good: a named witness, a specific setting, published while plenty of people who knew Wilde were alive to object. It still isn’t Wilde’s handwriting.
detailsBody: We reserve “verified” for lines we can point to inside a work the author actually wrote, or a transcript of what they actually said. Quote Investigator ↗ looked and reports that it has not located this jape in Wilde’s writings — while also concluding that there is evidence he employed it.

Quote Investigator adds one useful dating note: Wilde was in jail from 1895 to 1897 and his social circumstances changed dramatically afterward, so if he used the quip at all he probably said it before 1895 — some fifteen years before Hicks printed it.
context.pull: Wilde died in 1900. The line first reached print in 1910 — in someone else’s book.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article states the earliest ascription of "It is the best play I ever slept through" to Oscar Wilde that it located was published in 1911 in Seymour Hicks's memoir Twenty-Four Years of an Actor's Life (John Lane, New York, quote page 132), and concludes it has not located the jape in Wilde's writings although there is evidence he employed it.

The same Quote Investigator article documents the earliest printed instance of the joke as an 1898 Denver Evening Post report of Rev. Myron W. Reed's sermon ("It was the most exhaustive lecture I ever slept through"), plus 1922 (picture), 1923 Will Rogers/Boston Globe (Messages), 1929 (opera) and 1937 (Baccalaureate service) variants, and reports that Hesketh Pearson's 1946 Oscar Wilde: His Life and Wit, page 196, names Arthur Pinero as the target.

The Internet Archive scan of Seymour Hicks: Twenty-Four Years of an Actor's Life contains, on page 132, the passage "It was Wilde who, on being asked on returning from a fashionable premiere how he liked the piece, replied: 'My dear friend, it is the best play I ever slept through.'" The title page reads LONDON: ALSTON RIVERS LIMITED, 1910, with "FIRST PUBLISHED October 26th, 1910." The item metadata lists possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.
Wikipedia states Oscar Wilde lived 16 October 1854 – 30 November 1900 and was an Irish author, poet and playwright, among the most popular dramatists in London in the early 1890s.

Wikipedia states Seymour Hicks (30 January 1871 – 6 April 1949) was a British actor, music hall performer, playwright, actor-manager and producer, and lists his autobiography Seymour Hicks: 24 Years of an Actor's Life (Alston Rivers, London) under Further reading.
A fetch of Wikiquote's Oscar Wilde page finds no occurrence of the phrase "slept through" anywhere on it — the line is listed in none of its sections (Sourced, Attributed or Misattributed).

Wikipedia states Sir Arthur Wing Pinero (24 May 1855 – 23 November 1934) was an English playwright and early in his career an actor, and notes his The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893) was scheduled to replace Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan at the St James's Theatre.
